hero.title: Learn Armenian in Los Angeles
hero.subtitle: Greater LA is home to the largest Armenian population outside Armenia itself. Whether you're reconnecting with family, raising kids who hear Armenian at home, or just live down the street from Little Armenia, Haylingua gives you a real way to learn — free, online, at your own pace.

community.heading: A community you can hear on the street
community.intro: From Glendale to East Hollywood's officially designated Little Armenia, Armenian isn't a foreign language in LA — it's on storefront signs, church bulletins, and restaurant menus. That makes it one of the easiest places in the world to go from lessons to real conversation.

landmarks.title: Glendale
landmarks.text: Often called the heart of the LA Armenian community, with Armenian-owned bakeries, bookstores, and community centers throughout the city.

landmarks.title: Little Armenia, East Hollywood
landmarks.text: An official City of Los Angeles cultural district, packed with Armenian restaurants, markets, and shops.

landmarks.title: St. Leon Armenian Cathedral
landmarks.text: The seat of the Western Diocese of the Armenian Church, in Burbank, at the center of community life for generations of Angelenos.

landmarks.title: Abril Bookstore
landmarks.text: A longtime Glendale institution for Armenian-language books, music, and film — a great place to find reading material once you've built your basics.

whyLearn.heading: Why now is the right time
whyLearn.text: If you grew up hearing Armenian at home but never quite learned to read or write it, or you married into the community, or you're a heritage speaker whose Armenian is stronger in conversation than in the alphabet — LA gives you constant, low-pressure chances to practice everything Haylingua teaches you, from ordering at a bakery to following a church service.

losAngeles.faqHeading: Questions from Armenian learners in LA

faq.q: Do people in LA speak Western or Eastern Armenian?
faq.a: Mostly Western Armenian — LA's community largely descends from Genocide survivors and refugees from the Ottoman Empire and the broader Middle East. Haylingua currently teaches Standard Eastern Armenian (the form spoken in Armenia today), which shares the same alphabet and much of the grammar and vocabulary, but differs in pronunciation of certain letters. It's still an excellent foundation, and many LA heritage speakers use it to formally learn to read and write for the first time.

faq.q: I already understand spoken Armenian from my family — can Haylingua still help?
faq.a: Yes — heritage speakers often have strong listening comprehension but never learned to read or write. Haylingua's alphabet course and typing exercises are built exactly for filling that specific gap.

faq.q: Is there a way to practice with real people, not just an app?
faq.a: Absolutely — LA's density of Armenian churches, cultural centers, and businesses means you'll have real chances to use what you learn almost immediately, which is one of the best ways to make it stick.
